amendment.text: Anchorage does not use the state's plumbing-code table. It deletes Section 422 of the Uniform Plumbing Code and counts toilets by Table 2902.1 of the 2024 International Building Code, with one change: in each toilet room urinals may replace no more than 67 percent of the required toilets (in every occupancy). The rest of Section 2902 is unamended: half men and half women, round up, single-user rooms count and must be identified as available to all persons, separate rooms not required at 15 occupants or fewer, in mercantile at 100 or fewer and in business at 25 or fewer, and a multi-user room for all persons is allowed with privacy at toilets and urinals, counted on 100 percent of the occupants.
amendment.quote: [AMC 23.25.422] Delete section 422. Refer to the International Building Code. [AMC 23.15 Table 2902.1] Amend Table 2902.1 as follows: Under the WATER CLOSETS column: Replace "URINALS SEE SECTION 424.2 OF THE INTERNATIONAL PLUMBING CODE" with "In each bathroom or toilet room, urinals shall not be substituted for more than 67 percent of the required water closets." [2024 IBC Table 2902.1, secondary copy] Restaurants, banquet halls and food courts: 1 per 75 [male] / 1 per 75 [female]. Business: 1 per 25 for the first 50 and 1 per 50 for the remainder exceeding 50. Educational facilities: 1 per 50. [2902.1.1] To determine the occupant load of each sex, the total occupant load shall be divided in half. [...] Fractional numbers resulting from applying the fixture ratios of Table 2902.1 shall be rounded up to the next whole number. [...] Exceptions: [...] 2. Where multiple-user facilities are designed to serve all genders, the minimum fixture count shall be calculated 100 percent, based on total occupant load. [2902.2 exceptions] 2. Separate toilet facilities shall not be required in structures or tenant spaces with a total occupant load, including both employees and customers, of 15 or fewer. 3. [...] in mercantile occupancies in which the maximum occupant load is 100 or fewer. 4. [...] in business occupancies in which the maximum occupant load is 25 or fewer. [Table note d] The occupant load for seasonal outdoor seating and entertainment areas shall be included when determining the minimum number of facilities required.

worked_examples.how: 25 women, 25 men. 1 per 25 for the first 50: 1 each. 67% of 1 is less than 1, so no urinal can replace the men's toilet. A business occupancy of 25 or fewer may have one shared room (2902.2 exception 4).
50 each. 1 per 25 for the first 50: 2 each. Up to 1 of the men's 2 may be a urinal (67% of 2 = 1.34).
100 each. 2 for the first 50, plus 1 per 50 for the remaining 50: 3 each. Up to 2 of the men's 3 may be urinals.
200 each. 2 for the first 50, plus 150/50 = 3: 5 each. Up to 3 of the men's 5 may be urinals (67% of 5 = 3.35).
100 each. 100/75 = 1.33, rounds up to 2 each. Up to 1 of the men's 2 may be a urinal.
200 each. 200/75 = 2.67, rounds up to 3 each. Up to 2 of the men's 3 may be urinals.
100 each. 100/50 = 2 each. Up to 1 of the boys' 2 may be a urinal.
200 each. 200/50 = 4 each. Up to 2 of the boys' 4 may be urinals (67% of 4 = 2.68).

fixtures.note: The 2024 International Building Code text (Table 2902.1, Sections 2902.1.1 to 2902.4, 1210.3.1, 1210.3.2) was read on UpCodes' copy published as the Wyoming Building Code 2024, which showed no state amendment in those sections; the Anchorage amendments were read on the municipality's own PDFs. The urinal figures in worked_examples (urinals_allowed) are arithmetic on the 67 percent cap, not a table in the code.

restrooms_city.rule: No separate restroom ordinance was found. The rules come from the building code Anchorage adopted: single-user toilet rooms must be identified as available to all persons regardless of sex; a multi-user room designed for all persons may replace separate men's and women's rooms where toilets and urinals have privacy; public toilet rooms need a sign saying whether they are for males, females or all persons. The Anchorage Equal Rights Commission states that discrimination by sex or gender identity or expression in public accommodations is illegal in Anchorage (Anchorage Municipal Code Title 5).
restrooms_city.quote: [2024 IBC 2902.1.2] Single-user toilet facilities and bathing rooms, and family or assisted-use toilet facilities and bathing rooms shall be identified as being available for use by all persons regardless of their sex. [2902.2 exception 6] Separate toilet facilities shall not be required where rooms having both water closets and lavatory fixtures are designed for use by all persons regardless of sex and privacy is provided for water closets in accordance with Section 405.3.4 of the International Plumbing Code and for urinals in accordance with Section 405.3.5 of the International Plumbing Code. [2902.4] Required public toilet facilities shall be provided with signs that indicate whether the facility is to be used by males, by females, or by all persons regardless of sex. [1210.3.1] Each water closet utilized by the public or employees shall occupy a separate compartment with walls or partitions and a door enclosing the fixtures to ensure privacy. [1210.3.2] Each urinal utilized by the public or employees shall occupy a separate area with walls or partitions to provide privacy. The walls or partitions shall begin at a height not more than 12 inches (305 mm) from and extend not less than 60 inches (1524 mm) above the finished floor surface. [AERC] AERC enforces local anti-discrimination laws covering: [...] Public accommodations (e.g., businesses, services, facilities) [...] It's illegal in Anchorage to discriminate based on race, color, sex, gender identity or expression, sexual orientation, religion, national origin, marital status, age, or physical and mental disability.
restrooms_city.note: Exception 6 points to International Plumbing Code Sections 405.3.4 and 405.3.5, which Anchorage does not adopt (references to that code mean the Uniform Plumbing Code under AMC 23.10.101.6). The same privacy rules are in the building code itself, Sections 1210.3.1 and 1210.3.2. Anchorage Municipal Code Title 5 itself was not read (the code site, ecode360, refused automated access).

page.meta: Commercial bathroom partitions delivered to Anchorage job sites. Price your restroom, pick a material and see the Anchorage building rules that apply.
page.lead: Commercial bathroom partitions for Anchorage offices, schools, clinics and air cargo warehouses, shipped by freight to your job site.
page.access_bullet: - **Wheelchair access:** a restroom with stalls needs at least one stall a wheelchair user can enter and use. Federal law and Anchorage's building rules set the sizes.
page.fire_bullet: - **Fire safety:** Anchorage's building rules require solid plastic (HDPE) used as an interior finish to pass a room fire test. Ask for the fire-rated version.
page.stall_bullet: - **How many stalls:** Anchorage sets the number of toilets by how many people use the building. The table below shows what that means.
page.state_extra_bullet: - **Anchorage extras:** accessible stalls here need a second, upright grab bar on the side wall, and a wheelchair stall needs more toe room under its partitions (12 inches high, against 9 under the federal rules). In a large restroom, 5% of the stalls must be wheelchair accessible, not just one. Restaurants, venues and stores that need six or more toilets also need a family restroom.
page.restroom_bullet: - **Single-user and all-gender restrooms:** Anchorage's building rules require a one-person restroom to be marked as open to everyone, whatever their sex. They allow a shared all-gender room in place of separate men's and women's rooms if every toilet has its own stall with a door and every urinal is screened. A public restroom needs a sign saying whether it is for men, for women or for everyone. The Anchorage Equal Rights Commission enforces the city's law against discrimination by sex or gender identity in businesses and other places open to the public.
page.permit_bullet: - **Permits:** Anchorage requires a permit to alter or repair a building and lists the work that needs none. The list covers painting, papering, tiling, carpeting, cabinets, countertops and similar finish work, and movable partitions no taller than 5 feet 9 inches that aren't fixed in place. It doesn't name toilet partitions fixed to the floor or wall, so ask the Development Services permit counter (907-343-8211) whether your replacement needs one. In the parts of the municipality outside the Anchorage Building Safety Service Area, the city's code makes applying for a building permit optional. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.confirm_office: the Municipality of Anchorage Development Services Department
page.stalls_intro: Anchorage's building rules count toilets by a building's capacity: the most people it is designed to hold at one time, worked out from its floor area. It isn't the number of staff or of visitors in a day. Half are counted as men and half as women. Every toilet needs a stall, and every urinal needs a screen on each side. Urinals are optional: in a men's room they may replace up to two thirds of the toilets, so the table shows the men's side as stalls.
page.stalls_after: These are Anchorage's minimums for the whole building, and at least one stall in each room must be wheelchair accessible. A men's room that needs only one toilet can't swap it for a urinal. An office designed for 25 people or fewer, a store for 100 or fewer, or any space for 15 or fewer, may have one shared restroom instead of separate men's and women's rooms. A shared all-gender room is counted on everyone in the building instead of half. A restaurant's seasonal outdoor seating counts toward the number of people. Anchorage counts toilets by its own building rules, so these numbers differ from the ones Alaska's plumbing rules give for the rest of the state.
page.capacity: To find your building's capacity, Anchorage's building rules count an office at one person per 150 square feet of floor, a restaurant dining room at one per 15 square feet and a classroom at one per 20.
skip_state_sources: Floor area per person and a stall for every toilet
stall rules beyond the federal ones
Single-user restroom signs and separate rooms
page.install_rule: Anchorage requires anyone engaged in construction in its service area to hold a Municipal Contractor's License as well as a State of Alaska contractor registration, and the city's code applies that rule even to work that needs no permit. An owner or tenant of a commercial property may use its own employees for alteration work on that property. Alaska requires every contractor, including specialty installers, to hold a state contractor registration, with bond and insurance, before bidding or working. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.faq_install_extra: A contractor working in Anchorage needs a State of Alaska contractor registration and a Municipal Contractor's License.
page.public_jobs_bullet: - **Public jobs:** on state, city, borough and school district construction contracts over $25,000, Alaska law requires at least the wage rates the state labor department publishes for the region. For a journeyman carpenter in Anchorage that is $52.54 an hour plus $28.21 in benefits.
page.sales_tax_bullet: - **Sales tax:** none in Anchorage. Alaska has no state sales tax, and Anchorage has no general sales tax: its retail sales taxes apply only to alcoholic beverages and marijuana.
page.tax_install_bullet: - **Tax on installation:** Alaska has no state sales tax and Anchorage has no general sales tax, so none is added to installation labor in Anchorage.
page.tax_ship_bullet: - **Buying without installation:** partitions shipped to an Anchorage address carry no state or city sales tax. Elsewhere in Alaska a city or borough may have its own sales tax, and it follows the delivery address.
page.tax_confirm: your accountant or the Municipality of Anchorage Treasury Division
page.buyers_extra: - **Airport, air cargo and military buildings:** HDPE or phenolic where restrooms take hard use around the clock, stainless steel in public terminals.
